nodes.title: Generative AI concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Generative AI models produce new content (text, images, code) from prompts. AWS AIF-C01 tests foundational concepts: how foundation models work, prompt engineering basics, responsible AI, and key AWS AI services.

flashcards.back: A large model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks via fine-tuning or prompting — e.g., Amazon Titan, Anthropic Claude.
Pairs an FM with a knowledge base: retrieves relevant documents at query time and injects them into the prompt, reducing hallucinations on private/recent data.
Zero-shot: prompt only; no examples. Few-shot: include 2-5 examples in the prompt to guide the model's output format or style.
Serverless API access to multiple FMs from different providers (Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Amazon) without managing infrastructure.

questions.q: A team is integrating a large language model into a customer-support assistant. They notice that small changes in how they word the request — adding examples, specifying tone, asking the model to think step by step — dramatically change the output quality without changing model weights. Which discipline are they applying?
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing a model's text input — instructions, examples, formatting and step-by-step cues — so a foundation model produces accurate, on-task output without altering its weights. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller model to mimic a larger one. RLHF tunes model weights using human preference signals during a training stage, not at request time. Hyperparameter tuning searches training settings such as learning rate; all three change the model or its training rather than the prompt.

questions.q: A product team has a public LLM that has no knowledge of internal product manuals updated last week. They want answers grounded in those manuals without retraining the model. Their solution: index the manuals, retrieve top passages by similarity at request time, and inject them into the prompt as context. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) indexes documents, retrieves the most relevant passages by similarity at request time and injects them into the prompt as context, grounding answers in private or fresh data without retraining. RLHF tunes model weights from human preference data. Knowledge distillation compresses a large model into a smaller one. Few-shot prompting adds a few example pairs to the prompt but has no retrieval step over an external corpus.

questions.q: A company evaluating generative-AI patterns wants a precise definition of a foundation model so non-technical stakeholders can contrast it with other ML approaches such as narrow classifiers, rules engines and federated training. Which option BEST describes a foundation model?
choices: A handcrafted rules engine assembled by domain experts, with no statistical training and no ability to generalize beyond its rules
A narrow single-task model trained from scratch on a small labelled dataset for one specific business objective
A federated learning algorithm that trains a model only on edge devices to preserve raw data privacy by design
A large model pretrained on broad unlabelled data, then adapted to many tasks via prompting, RAG or fine-tuning
questions.explanation: A foundation model is a large model pretrained on broad, mostly unlabelled data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks — text, code, images — via prompting, RAG or fine-tuning. A narrow single-task model is the opposite: trained on a small labelled set for one job. A handcrafted rules engine has no statistical training component. Federated learning is a distributed training approach for private data, not a definition of a foundation model.

questions.q: A bank already has a public LLM answering well over their indexed compliance manuals via retrieval-augmented generation. Now they want the model itself to adopt their specific tone, terminology, and structured response format consistently across all answers — beyond what context injection achieves. When should fine-tuning be preferred over RAG?
choices: When the underlying knowledge changes daily, so the model can absorb each update without an index rebuild
When the assistant must store a small list of frequently-changing policy values, since fine-tuning reliably memorizes those facts verbatim
When the model itself must consistently adopt a specific tone, vocabulary and response format across every answer it produces
When inference cost is the priority, since a fine-tuned model never benefits from caching retrieved passages
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning is preferred when the model itself must consistently adopt a stable behaviour — tone, domain vocabulary or response format — across all answers, beyond what prompt context alone can guarantee. Fine-tuning does not reliably memorize discrete facts; it teaches patterns and style, and changing facts still belong in a retrieval index. For knowledge that changes frequently, RAG is better because you update only the document store. And fine-tuning is not automatically cheaper at inference: it carries training cost up front and must be repeated whenever the desired behaviour changes.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
